title: operator-decision-playbook-rate-limits-timeouts
content:
Purpose: Quick operator decision playbook for common API degradations (client timeouts, 429s, degraded streaming, elevated error rates). This is intentionally pragmatic: short checks, conservative mitigations, and escalation triggers. Meant to be copied into pager messages and used during first 20 minutes of an incident.

Scope: Applies to inference edge services (api-gateway, inference-proxy, runtime-frontend) and associated ingress/load-balancers. Not intended for long-running postmortem analysis (see postmortem template).

Signals that should trigger using this playbook:
- Sudden spike in 429 rate (>1% of requests in 1m) or sustained 5m > 0.5% when baseline <<0.1%
- Error rate (5xx) p95 over last 5min > 1% or p50 latency regresses > 30% of baseline
- Streaming sessions with partial payloads, repeated client disconnects, or streaming latency > 3s for first chunk
- Upstream timeouts (runtime timeouts) increasing or redis/memcache timeouts observed

Quick triage (first 3–5 min)
1) Confirm scope: are all regions/tiers affected? Run:
   - Check SLO dashboards + compare regional filters
   - PromQL examples:
     - error_rate = sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api-gateway",status=~"5.."}[1m])) by (region)
     - rate_429 = sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api-gateway",status="429"}[1m])) by (region)
2) Correlate deploys/rollouts: check deploy activity in last 30m (deploys, canaries).
   - git: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/actions
   - Jira: SRE-842, DEPLOY-2100
3) Identify client vs server problem: Are client-side retries increasing? Look at ingress logs for x-forwarded-for and retry headers.

Minimal mitigation decision matrix (operator cheat sheet)
- If 429s concentrated to single customer or API key: apply per-customer rate-limit raise / temporary quota increase OR notify CS to throttle traffic at client.
- If 429s widespread but capacity OK: enable broader looser burst capacity (temporarily increase token-bucket burst) on gateway and schedule controlled backpressure downstream.
- If timeouts increased and backpressure visible: reduce model batch sizes, lower max-concurrent inference per worker, enable degraded model variant (quantized / smaller context) as fallback.
- If streaming degraded: reduce chunk size and increase socket keepalive; if proxy CPU is saturated, shift traffic away from affected proxies.

Diagnostic commands & quick checks
- tail ingress logs for 429 patterns:
  kubectl -n prod logs -l app=api-gateway --tail=200 | grep "status=429" | head -n 100
- check runtime worker latency and health:
  kubectl -n runtime get pods -l app=runtime-frontend -o wide
  kubectl -n runtime exec -it <pod> -- curl -sS localhost:9000/healthz
- tracing: sample traces with high latency and follow downstream spans (zipkin/jaeger link)
- check cache (redis) timeouts:
  redis-cli -h redis.public cluster info | grep -i timeout
- examine LB metrics (AWS ALB / GCP LB) for 5xx origin failures and backend connection errors

Mitigation recipes (concrete steps)
A) Widespread 429s and gateway saturated
  - Step 1: Switch api-gateway to progressive rejection mode (config flag: gateway.reject_mode=progressive) to emit structured fallback payloads rather than opaque 429s.
  - Step 2: Temporarily lift per-route burst limit by 30% for 15 minutes (monitor). Command: terraform apply -var=route_burst_override=true (have ops approval) OR use runtime console quick patch.
  - Step 3: Enable degraded-mode for heavy models: route /v1/generate to model-small variant (via routing policy tag: fallback=small).
  - Step 4: Schedule controlled rejections to keep p95 latency stable and protect throughput.

B) Elevated backend (runtime) timeouts
  - Step 1: Check GPU nodes and runtime queues for stuck requests (kubectl logs and runtime admin API).
  - Step 2: If queue depth high, scale up runtime pool by +20% using autoscale play (redwoodctl scale runtime --delta 0.2) or trigger burst nodes.
  - Step 3: If scaling not possible, enable per-request execution timeout reduction and short-circuit long requests (config: runtime.exec_timeout_ms=120000 -> 90000).
  - Step 4: If repeated model OOMs or EOS hangs, revert to last known-good model revision for that route.

C) Degraded streaming (chunk delays, partial sends)
  - Step 1: Check proxy worker CPU and network: top on proxy nodes; check egress bandwidth.
  - Step 2: Temporarily increase nginx/proxy proxy_read_timeout and keepalive (but short-term only): set proxy_read_timeout=60s -> 90s for suspect pool.
  - Step 3: If chunking itself fails, enable socket-level buffering bypass for streaming route (config toggle) to prefer smaller continuous writes.
  - Step 4: For client-visible corruption, enable monotonic fallback: return final non-streaming blob with note "stream degraded".

Retries & client guidance
- Never blindly retry on 5xx/timeout unless idempotent and with exponential backoff (initial 50ms, factor 2, jitter).
- For 429, advise clients to honor Retry-After header. If missing, use exponential backoff and a cap at 60s.
- For streaming: prefer resumable tokens rather than naive reconnects; recommend client implement linear backoff with jitter for reconnect attempts.

Escalation criteria (who to page)
- Page SRE primary if: error rate > 3% sustained for 10m OR widespread p95 latency > 5s for 10m.
- Page infra on-call if GPU node health < 80% ready or scaling fails.
- Page product/PD if customer-impacting change was rolled in last 60m.

Rollback & post-incident actions
- If mitigation involves config change: keep change for 15m and validate; if metrics return to baseline revert to earlier config with note. Avoid flip-flopping more than twice.
- Post-incident: fill incident template (linked PM doc), attach key traces, list root cause hypotheses and confirm owners for follow-ups.

Operational knobs cheat-list (what we can flip quickly)
- gateway.reject_mode (progressive|strict)
- route_burst_override (percent)
- runtime.exec_timeout_ms
- runtime.fallback_variant (small|quantized|experimental)
- proxy.keepalive_timeout, proxy_read_timeout
- model_batch_max_tokens, model_concurrency_per_worker
- cache.ttl_override for prefix caching

Metrics & dashboards to check (prometheus / datadog names)
- http_requests_total{job="api-gateway"} (status labels)
- runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket (by model, route)
- streaming_chunk_latency_seconds
- redis_command_duration_seconds and redis_timeouts_total
- model_queue_depth_gauge

Common root causes we've seen
- Natural traffic spike from large customer or crawler (bad client behaviour)
- Recent model or runtime deploy that increased memory/latency cost
- Redis/memcache eviction storms causing cache misses and backend pressure
- Load-balancer health check misconfiguration that routes traffic to draining pods
- Connection pool exhaustion at the proxy layer

Run results template (fill in during incident)
- Incident start: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC
- Observed signal: (e.g., region us-west p95 latency 6s, 429 rate 2%)
- First action taken: (who, what, time)
- Temporary mitigations: (list)
- Outcome after 15m: (improved / unchanged / worse)
- Escalations: (paged who)
- Follow-ups assigned: (owner: action)

Postmortem checklist
- Collect top 20 traces that showed the highest latencies
- Reproduce load pattern in staging if possible
- Evaluate whether autoscale/burst knobs were effective or insufficient
- Create JIRA for long-term fix and link to incident (SRE-842 style)

Notes to self / rough ideas (brainstorm, do not block ops)
- Consider automatic local-circuit-breaker that reduces model concurrency on error spike and toggles fallback variant automatically.
- Track per-customer historical burst tolerance to avoid global 429 events from one bad actor.
- Add a streaming health header that clients can poll to avoid frequent reconnect churn.

Open questions (to review with runtime/product)
- Should we expose a safe-mode API flag for customers to opt into degraded but cheaper model paths during incidents?
- What is the right default for retry-backoff in SDKs? (current SDK uses 200ms initial)
- Is there appetite to add automatic transient TTL increases on prefix caches to reduce backend pressure during traffic surges?

References & links
- Related incident notes: github.com/redwood-inference/ops-notes/issues/58
- Deployment roll history: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/releases
- Circuit breaker proto: engineering/designs/circuit-breaker-v2.md (confluence)

Bottom line: stay conservative in mitigations—protect latency SLOs and keep a single owner for any config flips. Priority ordering: 1) prevent collapse of p95 latency, 2) open routes for critical customers if safe, 3) avoid long-term config churn without follow-up.

Last edited by: Maya Chen
